items.title: Most adult humans can't digest milk — and that's normal
items.claim: Babies make lactase to digest lactose in milk. In most of the world's adults, lactase production switches off after weaning. Adult milk-drinkers — common in Europeans and some African and Middle Eastern populations — carry a recently evolved mutation.

options.text: Adult lactose intolerance is ancestral; lactase persistence is a derived trait that arose in populations that domesticated dairy animals in the last 10,000 years

items.reveal:
Roughly 65 percent of adult humans globally show reduced lactase production after weaning. Lactase persistence is most common in northern Europeans (around 90 percent), some West African pastoralist groups, and some Middle Eastern populations.

Different regulatory mutations independently produced this trait in different lineages — convergent evolution. The European variant (a single nucleotide change near the LCT gene, called T-13910) is dated to about 5,000 to 10,000 years ago, coinciding with cattle domestication.

Dairy farming and lactase persistence appear to have co-evolved: ancient DNA shows farmers drank milk before persistence was common, suggesting cultural use (fermented dairy, lower lactose) preceded biological adaptation. As populations relied more on milk, the persistence allele was strongly selected.
items.why: European diets are taken as a baseline; lactose intolerance is treated as a disorder. Globally, lactose intolerance IS the baseline — milk drinking adults are the rare ones.

items.title: Elephants need hairs to STAY COOL
items.claim: Big animals are well-insulated by sheer size — surface area to volume ratio drops as you scale up. So why do elephants have sparse but persistent hairs, in a hot environment where insulation is the last thing they need?
items.prompt: What's the function of an elephant's hairs?

options.text: They INCREASE convective heat loss — the sparse hairs disrupt the still air layer at the skin surface and allow more efficient cooling than bare skin would

items.reveal_title: Surface area scaling and thermal management
items.reveal:
Animal mass scales as length cubed; surface area as length squared. Doubling an animal's linear size doubles its surface-to-volume ratio's inverse — large animals have proportionally less surface area to dump heat through.

Elephants generate huge metabolic heat (about 2500 watts at rest for a 4 tonne adult) but have proportionally tiny skin. They are constantly battling overheating. Their hairs, ears (huge for their body), wallowing in mud, and behavioural cooling all serve heat dissipation.

Cordeschi and colleagues (2012) modelled elephant hair density and showed sparse hairs improve heat loss by about 5 to 20 percent — likely a real evolutionary purpose.
items.why: Hair is associated with warmth. For animals at the wrong end of the surface-to-volume scaling, hair can do the opposite.
